newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Verplaetse to replace Duisenberg as BIS president.
newsitem.headline: Verplaetse to replace Duisenberg as BIS president.

text.p: Alfons Verplaetse, governor of the Belgian National Bank (BNB), will replace Wim Duisenberg, president of the Dutch central bank, as the next president and chairman of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS).
BIS, central bank to the worlds' central banks, said on Monday its board of directors elected Verplaetse as president and chairman for period of three years starting on July 1.
Duisenberg's term at BIS was due to expire at the end of June when he takes over as president of the European Monetary Institute (EMI), the forerunner of the European Central Bank (ECB).
Under Duisenberg, BIS moved rapidly to boost its global presence and last year it added nine new central banks to join the 32-member organisation.
The nine new members are Russia, China, India, Hong Kong, Singapore, South Korea, Saudi Arabia, Brazil and Mexico.
Verplaetse, 67, was named governor of the Belgian central bank in July 1989 following his appointment as director of the central bank in 1985.
Between 1982 and 1988 he was also director of the Cabinet of the Belgian prime minister, where he played a key role in the recovery of the Belgian economy.

For many years Verplaetse was also member of the working group of monetary experts that reported monthly to the Committee of Governors of the Central Banks of the Member States of the European Community.

Last month Verplaetse was re-appointed for a limited one year period as governor because he has passed the official retirement age. His term at BNB is expected to be rolled over again next year, but it is widely anticipated that he will retire by February 1999.
If Verplaetse were to retire from the Belgian central bank before the end of his three-year term at BIS, he would also have to step down from his position at BIS.
Duisenberg, who also will be retiring from the Dutch central bank on June 30, has been president of BIS twice, the first man to hold the position for two terms.

He was initially president from 1988 to December 1990 when he was replaced by Bengt Dennis, governor of Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank. Duisenberg was then re-elected for another three-year term in December 1993. His term was later extended to expire in June.
"As chairman and president he has guided the bank (BIS) with skilful and firm leadership and has reinforced its role as a forum for cooperation among central banks," BIS said in a statement.

BIS added its board expressed its "deep gratitude for the outstanding services he has rendered to the Bank during his 15 years as a member of the board." BIS's board of directors is made up of central bank governors from the Group of 10 (G10) leading industrial nations, who meet to discuss international monetary and financial issues at BIS's tower-like headquarters in Basle 10 times a year.
G10 in fact comprises 11 countries: the U.S., Japan, Germany, Canada, France, Britain, Italy, the Netherlands, Belgium, Sweden and Switzerland.
But it is only since 1994, when the U.S., Japan and Canada took up their seats on the BIS board that the G10 and the BIS board have been identical.
Prior to this move, the BIS board was purely European.
Traditionally, the presidency of BIS is held by a central banker from one of the smaller European countries.
Since the mid-1960s, for example, the presidency of BIS has been held by central bankers from the Netherlands, Switzerland, Belgium and Sweden.
